article.title: htmx 4.0 Rewrites Its Request Engine on fetch(), Adds Built-In Morphing Swaps and Explicit Attribute Inheritance
article.summary: htmx 4.0.0 replaces XMLHttpRequest with fetch(), bakes in idiomorph DOM morphing, and makes attribute inheritance explicit, skipping version 3 entirely.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview The htmx team has released [htmx 4.0.0](https://github.com/bigskysoftware/htmx/releases/tag/v4.0.0), the first major version of the hypermedia library since 2.0 arrived in 2024, according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/). The release [landed on August 28](https://dev.to/jamilxt/htmx-40-just-shipped-what-changed-what-breaks-and-how-to-migrate-this-weekend-a4o) after eight months of work, and, as [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/) notes, it skips version 3 entirely. Creator Carson Gross, who had promised there would never be an htmx 3.0, summed up the jump to [InfoWorld](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4150864/htmx-4-0-hypermedia-finds-a-new-gear.html) in a one-word quote: "Oops." ## What We Know The core of the release is a transport swap: htmx now sends every request through the browser's native `fetch()` API instead of the `XMLHttpRequest` object it had used since its intercooler.js days, according to [InfoWorld](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4150864/htmx-4-0-hypermedia-finds-a-new-gear.html). The rewrite unlocks native response streaming while keeping the library at around [14KB](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/), and for most developers the familiar `hx-get` and `hx-post` attributes behave exactly as before, [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/) reports. Two features build directly on that rewrite. Morphing swaps powered by the idiomorph algorithm — also created by Gross — are now built into the core rather than shipped as an extension, preserving DOM state such as input focus during updates, [InfoWorld](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4150864/htmx-4-0-hypermedia-finds-a-new-gear.html) reports. And a new `` tag lets a single server response cleanly update multiple page targets, replacing the older out-of-band swap syntax, according to the [official htmx documentation](https://four.htmx.org/docs/whats-new-in-htmx-4). The release's biggest breaking change is that attribute inheritance is no longer implicit. In htmx 2, an attribute like `hx-confirm` set on a parent element silently applied to every htmx-driven child. In 4.0, attributes only inherit down the DOM tree when explicitly marked with an `:inherited` suffix, the [official documentation](https://four.htmx.org/docs/whats-new-in-htmx-4) confirms: ```
``` A migration write-up on [DEV Community](https://dev.to/jamilxt/htmx-40-just-shipped-what-changed-what-breaks-and-how-to-migrate-this-weekend-a4o) flags this as the change most likely to cause silent production breakage: an `hx-headers` attribute carrying a CSRF token down to child elements making `hx-delete` calls simply stops reaching those requests without the `:inherited` suffix, and "the server starts rejecting deletes with a 403. Nothing in the browser looks broken. The button renders, the request fires, the server says no." Other changes include a new default 60-second request timeout — htmx 2 had none, according to the [official documentation](https://four.htmx.org/docs/whats-new-in-htmx-4) — and event names standardized to a `htmx:phase:action` pattern, so `htmx:afterRequest` becomes `htmx:after:request`. History navigation no longer snapshots the DOM into `localStorage`; instead, back navigation re-fetches the page from the server, which [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/) says lets third-party scripts "just work." Attribute names were also reshuffled: `hx-disable` now does what `hx-disabled-elt` used to do, while the old meaning of `hx-disable` moves to a new `hx-ignore` attribute, per the [official documentation](https://four.htmx.org/docs/whats-new-in-htmx-4). To ease the transition, the team shipped a command-line checker that scans a codebase for inheritance issues, renamed attributes, and deprecated events, both [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/) and [DEV Community](https://dev.to/jamilxt/htmx-40-just-shipped-what-changed-what-breaks-and-how-to-migrate-this-weekend-a4o) note: ``` npx htmx.org@4.0.0 upgrade-check -- ./templates ``` The 4.0 line ships under npm's `next` tag rather than `latest`, so sites pulling htmx from an unversioned CDN link are not force-upgraded, and version 2.x remains supported indefinitely, according to [DEV Community](https://dev.to/jamilxt/htmx-40-just-shipped-what-changed-what-breaks-and-how-to-migrate-this-weekend-a4o). Reception on [Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49478178) was largely positive: the release thread had drawn more than 700 points, with commenters praising the combination of Go, SQLite, and htmx and how well AI coding assistants handle the library, [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/) reports — one commenter on the thread wrote that Claude "understands it and does it well." Not every reaction was positive: [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/) notes that some developers argued htmx mixes presentation with business logic and said their teams were migrating back to React. The [release notes on GitHub](https://github.com/bigskysoftware/htmx/releases/tag/v4.0.0) list more than 200 merged pull requests going into the release, including 12 contributors who made their first contribution to the project. ## What We Don't Know Neither [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/) nor the [official documentation](https://four.htmx.org/docs/whats-new-in-htmx-4) specifies exactly when npm's `latest` tag will shift from 2.x to 4.x, beyond the general framing that 2.x support continues indefinitely. It is also not yet clear how many production sites have adopted 4.0 since the August 28 release, or how the framework's adoption compares with competing hypermedia approaches like Hotwired's Turbo. ## About htmx htmx is an open-source library, maintained by Big Sky Software, that adds AJAX requests, CSS transitions, WebSockets, and server-sent events directly to HTML through element attributes, letting developers build interactive interfaces with minimal JavaScript, according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/htmx-4-released/). It remains popular with Django, Go, and Rails backends that favor server-rendered HTML over heavier client-side frameworks.
